summary.text:
Devon and Somerset Fire and Rescue Authority's Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27 to 2028-29 (Report DSFRA/26/6) is a 26-page substantive TMS taken by the Authority on 16 February 2026, from Andrew Furbear, Head of Finance (Treasurer) and Section 112 officer. All three appendices (Prudential and Treasury Indicators, MRP Statement, MUFG economic report) are bundled in the PDF. The companion Q3 Performance Report (RC/26/5, doc 12871, Resources Committee 5 February 2026) is held locally and is the only place a weighted loan rate, average life and count of external draws since 2012 are printed — the strategy paper itself does not carry those three data points.

The loan book reconciles cleanly. Our file, searched under the exact bc-loans name 'DEVON & SOMERSET FIRE & RESCUE AUTHORITY' (a naming trap: 'Devon and Somerset Fire and Rescue Authority' returns no match), holds 27 individual PWLB advances totalling £23,219,391 at a coupon-weighted 4.2505%, split 23 MATURITY and 4 EIP. RC/26/5 §5.8 (p6) prints external borrowing forecast at £23.219m at 31 March 2026 at a weighted 4.25% with an average life of 21.5 years, all fixed rate, and confirms no external loans since June 2012. Principal ties to the pound; rate ties to 2dp. The £47k gap between the 31.12.25 external of £23.266m (§3.2, p11) and the 31.3.26 forecast is consistent with the four EIP loans amortising over three months. §3.2 confirms the book is 100% PWLB — no LOBOs, no local-authority borrowing, no bank loans, matching our file exactly. The balance-sheet identity ties to the pound (or £1k rounding) at every forecast year-end: at 31.3.26, CFR £26,858k minus external borrowing £22,761k minus OLTL £2,482k equals £1,615k internal borrowing, and the paper prints '(1,615)' in the Under/Over borrowing line at §3.3 (p12).

The Authority runs simultaneously under-borrowed (external debt £1.615m below CFR at 31.3.26, per §3.3) and as a net treasury investor (£55.581m of investments against £23.266m of borrowing gives a net cash position of £32.315m at 31.12.25, per §3.2). §3.10 (p14) states outright 'there is no intention to take out any new borrowing during 2026-27 as the Authority can rely on its prudent Capital Reserve'; RC/26/5 §5.16 confirms no borrowing planned in 2025-26 either. The forward position changes in 2028-29: £13.569m of new borrowing is planned to fund an Estates capital programme step-up to £15.667m (§2.3, p7), which drives CFR up to £25.054m and flips the balance sheet to over-borrowed by £17.195m at year-end 31.3.29. Financing costs to net revenue rise across Appendix A's five-year horizon from 2.04% (2026-27) to 4.98% (2030-31). Investment activity: £1.434m of Q3 interest against a £1.2m full-year budget, 4.13% average yield outperforming 3-month SONIA by 12bp; only one placement (£5m to Kirklees at 4.30% maturing May 2027) sits beyond 365 days.

Two testable observations. First, on the DMO premature repayment curve dated 14 August 2026, our engine prices 25 of the 27 loans below par with a net indicative discount of £2.921m (12.6% of principal); the two short loans in the under-12-months bucket sit marginally above par. Paper §3.12 and RC/26/5 §5.9 both correctly state that on the repay-and-reborrow calculation there is no financial benefit — the premature repayment rate today sits above the equivalent new-borrowing rate for like tenors. That is a different test from repaying from reserves without reborrowing, which is the frame §3.10 and §5.16 explicitly set out. The discount finding is recorded here as an observation, never as advice, and no MRP or accounting treatment is modelled. Second, the paper's Appendix A maturity structure floor for 'under 12 months' during 2026-27 is set at 11%; our file shows 10.8% (£2.5m of £23.219m) as at 15 August 2026, marginally under the stated lower limit. Almost certainly a framing artefact rather than a breach — the limits were likely written before the two under-12m loans amortised into that bucket — but recorded for the file.

FRA precedent, from Avon (mg473) and Bedfordshire (mg288), has been to decline drafting a first-contact email on three grounds: audience (no FRA in the library's live drafts list has generated an email), address (no email printed for the Treasurer in the paper), and fit (small, net-investor books without the refinancing pressure the template's live hooks work on). Devon and Somerset fits (i) and (ii) exactly — Andrew Furbear is named as Head of Finance (Treasurer) and Section 112 officer but no email address is printed anywhere in either 12879 or 12871. On (iii) the fit is closer than Avon or Bedfordshire: 27 loans is a more diversified book than 1-2 loans, there is a genuine loan-book reconciliation to the pound and to 2dp on rate, and there is a substantive discount finding surfaced with the correct caveats. An email has been drafted per the session's instruction; the FRA precedent is flagged for consideration on whether to send.

officer.subject: Your paragraph 5.8 ties to our file to the pound
officer.body:
Andrew,

Apologies for the cold email — PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're a small platform that carries PWLB rates at both fixings each day, monthly local-authority-to-local-authority lending, every council and fire authority's PWLB loan book, and a lightweight academy for treasury officers. The data side is free and it will stay free. The one-page brochure is at pwlbtoday.com/brochure if it helps to circulate internally.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every authority in the country, so we can see how each authority's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. Below are some thoughts on your 16 February strategy paper and the 5 February Q3 performance report to Resources. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. The Q3 §5.8 line on the loan book is unusually complete, and this is offered in that spirit rather than as a critique.

That paragraph states £23.266m outstanding at 31 December 2025, forecast to reduce to £23.219m by 31 March 2026, weighted 4.25%, average life 21.5 years, all fixed rate. Our own file, pulled from the DMO borrower schedule under "DEVON & SOMERSET FIRE & RESCUE AUTHORITY", holds twenty-seven PWLB advances totalling £23,219,391 at a coupon-weighted 4.2505%. Principal ties to the pound with your year-end forecast, and the rate ties to two decimal places. Your strategy §3.2 also confirms the book is 100% PWLB — no LOBOs, no local-authority borrowing, no bank loans — which matches what we hold exactly. It's the cleanest loan-book reconciliation to a printed line we've had this month, so anything else below is grounded in the same file you are working from.

The observation worth passing back is on §3.12 in the strategy and §5.9 in the Q3. Both correctly say that on the repay-and-reborrow arithmetic there is no financial benefit — the PWLB premature repayment rate today sits above the equivalent new-borrowing rate for like tenors, and we get the same answer. What we can price separately is the different frame. Your strategy is explicit at §3.10 and §5.16 that the Authority is not reborrowing, and is funding capex from the Capital Reserve instead. On today's DMO premature repayment curve — notice 314/26 PM, 14 August 2026 — our engine prices twenty-five of the twenty-seven loans below par, with a net indicative discount of £2.92m across the book, or 12.6% of principal. Only the two short loans maturing in 2026 and 2027 stay marginally above par. This is indicative only — the DMO's quote is the only binding one, we model no MRP effect and no accounting treatment, and whether any of it is worth pursuing turns on the replacement cost of the cash and the timing of the Estates programme, both of which sit outside our model. It's a real number against a book that per your own strategy is not being reborrowed, and we've saved the workings against the paper so a walk-through is straightforward if useful.

The page that pulls all of this together is at pwlbtoday.com/pwlb-activity — every daily rate, every borrower, every maturity and an indicative break cost on the whole DMO curve.

The academy is a paid product with three courses that would fit — a Prudential and Treasury Code refresher pitched at fire-authority scale, a session on premature repayment and rescheduling arithmetic that covers the not-reborrow frame above, and a walkthrough of the Liability Benchmark. Free sign-up is at pwlbtoday.com/sign-up; the new-account discount runs until end of September.

If any of this lands, word of mouth is how we get in front of colleagues elsewhere — a mention to a peer treasurer in the region does more than any campaign we could run.

Best,
[NAME]
PWLBtoday
[LinkedIn]

Sources: DSFRA/26/6 Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27 to 2028-29 and RC/26/5 Treasury Management Performance 2025-26: Q3, both from Andrew Furbear, Head of Finance (Treasurer), at fireauthority.dsfire.gov.uk.

This draft is prepared per session instruction; whether to send is a broader question about whether the outreach opens to fire authorities at all. 2) Address needed — no email published for Andrew Furbear in either paper. 3) No forward treasury committee date is printed; sensible to time the send to the next Resources treasury item once its date appears in the queue. 4) Every figure in the draft ties to a paper page or to the price_book.py output at 2026-03-31 or 2026-08-15 — no derived or estimated numbers. 5) Draft runs 715 words against the ~650-word template target; the discount paragraph is the longest and could be tightened further if needed but the caveats are load-bearing. 6) The Appendix A under-12m / 10y+ floor observations (10.8% vs 11%, 80.8% vs 81%) were considered and dropped from the draft as edge-of-interesting; they sit in the note under maturity_structure if wanted. 7) Break-cost caveats follow the template: indicative only, DMO binds, no MRP, no accounting.
